en: The Sūtra on the Great Discernment of the Deviant and the Orthodox Spoken by the Buddha.
Chapter One: The Dharma-Gate of the Great Discernment of the Deviant and the Orthodox. Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was in the City of Universal Fragrance, presiding over a great assembly of followers as he preached the Dharma. Within it...

Within the city, there were further Bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Sovereign Mind-Controller Bodhisattva, Contemplator of the Two Kinds of Emptiness of the Body Bodhisattva, Contemplator of the Two Kinds of Reality of the Body Bodhisattva, Contemplator of the Impurity of the Body Bodhisattva, and Contemplator of the Absence of Defilement in the Body Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, beneath his seat were eighty-four thousand followers and bodhisattvas of the tenth stage.
Chapter Two: The Chapter on Bodhisattvas of the Tenth Stage. Why is this so?
What are the bodhisattvas of the ten stages?
First, the bodhisattva who has attained certainty in faith and severed doubt;
second, the bodhisattva who is able to advance in the practice of the path.
On the third stage, there are Bodhisattvas who constantly contemplate the severing of delusions;
on the fourth stage, Bodhisattvas who are constantly in samādhi without scattering their objects of focus;
and on the fifth stage, Bodhisattvas whose wisdom is fully perfected.
Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage are those who can rely upon the teachings and commands of their original masters;
bodhisattvas of the seventh stage are those who succeed to and establish the prior traditions;
bodhisattvas of the eighth stage are those who do not sever the essential nature of the Three Jewels.
The Bodhisattva of the Ninth Ground whose myriad practices are fully perfected;
the Bodhisattva of the Tenth Ground characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Chapter Three: The Request Made by Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. At that time, there was a bodhisattva within the assembly.
Named Mañjuśrī, he rose from his seat,
knelt with his right knee on the ground,
and joined his palms.
He addressed his original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, saying:
"All sentient beings, from the beginningless and vast kalpas past,
have transmigrated through the six realms of existence."
Wandering through birth and death without end,
they undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
As we reach this day,
we pray only that our original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha,
with great kindness and great compassion, will take pity upon all sentient beings.
To rescue and protect all sentient beings,
he briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for his assembly.
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī," [and continued:]
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
All sentient beings, from beginningless and vast kalpas past,
have transmigrated through the six realms of existence,
wandering through birth and death.
Without ever ceasing,
they have endured various sufferings and afflictions up until this very day.
All arise from the fundamental mind. Why is this?
Because the mind proceeds from one moment to the next.
Day after day,
month after month,
year after year.
The mind takes various objects as its conditions;
the emotions become defiled by worldly dust;
the mind is constantly in a state of distraction and lacks stability.
Therefore, the body is likewise so.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"You have now earnestly requested this."
"Consider this thoroughly:
what state of mind do you have?
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva replied:
Previously, out of earnest solicitation,
you briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of the assembly of disciples.
Those who did not yet know, we now hope that they may come to know.
I hope that those who have not yet awakened may awaken;
I hope that those who have not yet realized may realize;
I hope that those who have not yet attained mastery may attain mastery.
Those who have not yet realized Bodhi, I wish to cause them to realize Bodhi;
those who have not yet attained peace of mind, I wish to cause them to attain peace of mind.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
If you would study this sublime Dharma of settling the mind,
first return to take refuge in a true and virtuous spiritual friend. Why is this?
Those who do not yet know shall be made to know; they too must take refuge in a true spiritual friend.
Those who have not yet awakened shall be made to awaken; they too must take refuge in a true spiritual friend.
Those who have not yet realized shall be made to realize; they too must take refuge in a true spiritual friend.
Those who have not attained mastery should be led to mastery; they too must take refuge in a true spiritual friend.
Those who have not realized bodhi should be led to realize bodhi; they too must take refuge in a true spiritual friend.
Those who have not yet attained peace of mind should be led to attain it; they, too, ought to take refuge in a true and virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Chapter Four: The Discourse on Severing the Six Kinds of Views, Spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha for Bodhisattvas at the Initial Stage. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed Śākyamuni Buddha once more, saying:
Eighty-four thousand followers simultaneously made a vow, saying:
"We wish to take refuge in a true spiritual friend.
What practice should we first cultivate?"
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas,
or upāsikās who take refuge in a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),"
First one must sever the six realms of existence;
only then can one take refuge in a true spiritual friend. Why is this?
Regarding the six destinies:
first, one must not give rise to false conceptualization;
second, one must not deliberately deliberate upon right and wrong.
Third, one must not allow doubt or regret to arise in the mind.
Fourth, one must not harbor suspicion within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
Fifth, one must not give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Sixth, one must not claim that this contradicts the teachings;
only after first being able to sever these six types of views can one take refuge in a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Chapter Five: Cultivating the Path. At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha praised these true spiritual friends, saying they are inconceivable, immeasurable, and incomparable.
Fearing that the great assembly might give rise to doubt and regret,
thereby being unable to take refuge in a true spiritual friend,
he then spoke of his own past causes and conditions for the sake of the assembly.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"Listen as I speak of my own experience when I cultivated the Way while on the causal ground."
What merits have been attained?
What practices were cultivated to achieve the path of Buddhahood?
Recall my time in the past.
Throughout three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
one cultivates and studies conditioned merits,
which are fraught with many faults and afflictions.
They do not understand the principle of non-action;
instead, they seek by means of attachment to signs.
Consequently, for three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they undergo all manner of suffering and affliction.
Later, I encountered the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One at the Grove of Merit,
between the two śāla trees on Mount Pañcaśīrṣa within the city of Vaiśālī,
who briefly expounded for me the essentials of the Dharma.
I was then able to practice according to the instructions.
Furthermore, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored Ones and others instructed me to enter the Great Samantabhadra Maṇḍala within the city of Vaiśālī.
After forty-nine days— seven times seven— he attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
All virtues were perfected,
and he was adorned with a hundred blessings.
Having perfected and completed the myriad practices,
he subsequently attained the Way of Buddhahood;
the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One then rubbed my head and bestowed upon me a prediction of enlightenment.
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One said:
"I vow that you shall attain the Way in the future,
and your name shall be Śākyamuni Buddha, the Original Teacher."
He is eternally the compassionate father of all sentient beings through the four modes of birth and the guiding teacher of the six realms;
he dwells perpetually within the triple world to lead and receive those who are deluded.
Transmit this Dharma,
entrusting it to one another in succession so that it never be interrupted,
remaining as eternal and boundless as space.
Śākyamuni Buddha said:
"I vow not to transgress the instructions and commands of the Great Awakened World-Honored One;
for this reason, I shall transmit this Dharma and entrust it to one another in succession so that it never be interrupted."
Therefore, I now exhort the great assembly to skillfully draw near to true spiritual friends;
you will certainly obtain great benefit.
If you can practice according to these instructions,
you will attain the unsurpassed fruit in the future,
no different from me.
Chapter Six: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Inquiry on Great Benefit. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed Śākyamuni Buddha, saying:
"What is that which brings great benefit?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,
there is nothing that brings greater benefit than being able to transform all evil into all goodness."
"This is called great benefit.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked:
"What kind of person is able to transform all evil into all good?"
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,
there is none who can transform all evils into all virtues except for the true spiritual friend."
Why is this? Because a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is able to give rise to billions of skillful means and parables within the context of a single matter.
A spiritual friend is one who can destroy dualistic views and cause one to take refuge in the single essence.
A spiritual friend is...
One who can transform the evil minds of the three poisons into the single essence of the Triple Gem is a true spiritual friend;
such a person can subdue the four-poisoned evil snakes and thereby perfect the four modes of dignified conduct.
A virtuous friend is one who can transform the five poisons into the five precepts.
A virtuous friend is...
One who can restrain the six consciousnesses and observe the six fast days is a true spiritual friend;
such a person is able to seek the seven Buddhas within the midst of the seventh consciousness.
A spiritual friend is one who can transform the eight sufferings into the eight liberations.
A spiritual friend is...
One can transform deluded thoughts and inverted views into merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) can transform ignorance into the sun of wisdom.
A spiritual friend is one who can transform afflictions into bodhi.
A spiritual friend is...
A spiritual friend is one who can transform greed, anger, and delusion into the purity of the three karmas;
and who can transform malice and envy so that they become the four immeasurable minds.
A virtuous friend is one who can turn back the eight wrong paths and lead one into the factors of the Eightfold Noble Path.
A virtuous friend is...
It possesses great merit that is inconceivable, immeasurable, and incomparable;
were one to attempt to describe it in full, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
*Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-vinaya-prakaraṇa*, Chapter Seven: At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed Śākyamuni Buddha, saying:
“Disciple, I have a small doubt;
how may it be resolved?
Śākyamuni Buddha said:
Regarding what constitutes "minor doubt," Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva said:
"It refers to the wondrous Dharma of the Three Vehicles established by the Buddhas of the three periods of time."
Furthermore, he expounds tens of billions of skillful means to transform and guide all sentient beings,
causing them all to maintain a mind directed toward the Path.
"Why is it that all sentient beings wander restlessly through birth and death?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"Listen closely, listen closely."
Reflect upon this well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been wandering intensely through birth and death.
It is simply because they do not understand my meaning. Why is this?
If all sentient beings were to understand my meaning, they would be no different from me.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!
All sentient beings can only understand the Dharma-gate of the parable of the crushing."
"How could there be any sentient beings who would not gather here to hear my great eloquence on the profoundly subtle and wondrous Dharma of what is correct and what is false?
When the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī heard these words being spoken, he [responded].
He marveled at this unprecedented and inconceivable event;
furthermore, fear and apprehension arose in his heart,
and he reproached himself.
He threw his entire body to the ground,
falling unconscious;
after a long while, he regained consciousness.
Alas, what a long sigh!
How bitter and how painful!
Who would have expected that today we should encounter our Dharma-body parents?
He explained this sublime Dharma for settling the mind as well as its original causes and conditions.
He further expounded the profound and wondrous Dharma of Great Eloquence regarding the heterodox and the orthodox.
In the eighth chapter, "The Dharma-Door of Great Eloquence on the Heterodox and Orthodox," the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī again addressed his original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, saying:
Regarding the profound Dharma that distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox:
what is called "orthodox," and what is called "heterodox"?
The Buddha said, "Mañjuśrī,
the correct also has two kinds,
and the deviant also has two kinds."
Why is this? The meaning of these two kinds of perversions is extremely profound.
First, to seek characteristics apart from the essence is called being correct in the midst of the heterodox.
Second, not to believe that there is a Buddha within the body,
nor to believe that there is the Dharma within the body.
To be greedily attached to worldly affairs and to constantly act with perversion in accordance with causes and conditions is called "the most perverse among the perverse."
Regarding these two kinds of correctness,
their meaning is profoundly deep.
The first is to seek the characteristics apart from the substance and thereby realize that within one's own body there exists the three jewels as a single essence.
Furthermore, one knows that within the body there are merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
To possess within the body the faith that it contains the Tathāgatagarbha Dharma-body is called "the most correct among the correct."
Second, those who only recognize external objects and do not recognize their internal nature,
yet seek them while remaining attached to signs— this is called "correctness within error. Why is this?
Although I have previously explained four kinds of the heterodox and the orthodox,
there is only one matter that is truly real. Why is this?
For example, suppose there is a person who wishes to travel far to another land,
the distance of which may be over a million li,
and along whose path there are eighty-four thousand kinds of heterodox ways.
There is only one path that is true;
all other eighty-three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine paths are equally false.
There is only one path that is true.
"Regarding sentient beings who wish to cross over by means of the true path,
how can they reach their destination?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
If there are sentient beings who would travel upon the right path,
they must rely upon a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to establish a virtuous landmark, whereby they may reach their destination.
Why is this? For one who seeks the Way must first seek the One;
it is only by being able to establish the One as the fundamental principle that the method can be realized.
Within this, the Buddha established eighty-four thousand dharma-gates;
yet if one wishes to speak of the truth, they all ultimately return to the One. Why is this?
Ordinary beings and sages also become one.
Why is this? Because it is by seeking sagehood that one is an ordinary being.
It is like abandoning water while seeking ice;
that ice is water, and that water is ice.
Outside of ice there is no water;
outside of water there is no ice.
Thus, afflictions and bodhi likewise become one.
Why is this? To turn one's back on afflictions while seeking bodhi is like abandoning the form and seeking the shadow.
This is the form and yet it is the shadow;
this is the shadow and yet it is the form.
Outside the form there is no shadow.
Outside of the reflection there is no form;
thus, the mind and the Buddha also become one. Why is this?
To seek the Buddha while turning one's back on him is like seeking an echo while turning one's back on sound;
it is both that sound and its echo.
This echo is the sound;
outside of sound there is no echo,
and outside of echo there is no sound.
Non-coming is one;
"illusion" and "transformation" are two names.
What is it that is called "one"?
To explain this through analysis:
seeking it outside the body is entirely erroneous;
seeking it within the body constitutes becoming one with it.
Sentient beings have three types of conceptual discrimination;
therefore, the Buddha established the teachings and discipline of the Three Vehicles.
If one can thoroughly comprehend all phenomena, [one transcends these distinctions].
The three are also originally without three;
even one is empty, which is called "one.
Suddenly one awakens to the fact that the nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
To thoroughly understand ultimate quiescence and awaken to the unconditioned Great Way is what is truly called being wordless and unspeakable.
Chapter Nine: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Again Questions Regarding the Thirty-two Marks. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed Śākyamuni Buddha, saying:
He asked again, "What are the thirty-two marks?
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
"Listen attentively, listen attentively."
I shall now analyze and explain them for you.
Regarding the thirty-two marks,
there are two meanings.
The first is among ordinary beings,
where it is called the thirty-two kinds of inauspicious signs;
the second is among the noble ones.
These are called the thirty-two kinds of auspicious marks. Why is this?
As for the thirty-two kinds of inauspicious marks:
The body of an ordinary person possesses the eight sufferings;
the body of an ordinary person possesses the eight difficulties;
the body of an ordinary person possesses the eight doubts.
Within the bodies of ordinary beings, there are eight perversions.
Four times eight makes thirty-two, which are called the thirty-two kinds of evil marks.
Śākyamuni Buddha said:
It was also like this for me prior to encountering the Great Master during my stage as a practitioner; however,
ever since I have encountered the Great Master, it has been otherwise.
He then instructed me to transform these eight sufferings into the eight liberations,
these eight difficulties into the eight masteries,
and these eight doubts into the eight kinds of right faith.
Reversing these eight deviations, one returns to the Eightfold Noble Path.
Four times eight makes thirty-two; these are called the thirty-two kinds of auspicious marks. Why is this so?
Within these two marks, there are merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
they cannot be fully described.
Even if I were to describe them in detail, I would not reach the end even after the exhaustion of an eon.
Chapter Ten: Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Inquiry on the Eighty Minor Marks. At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva again addressed Śākyamuni Buddha, saying:
He asked again, "What are the eighty minor marks?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī,
"Listen attentively, listen attentively."
Reflect upon this well;
I shall now analyze and explain it for you.
As for the eighty secondary marks:
Its meaning is extremely profound.
Why is this? Because the severance of the ten unwholesome actions is what is termed the ten wholesome actions.
To sever and attain freedom from the five heinous crimes is called the "Five Reverent Obediences.
To restrain and master the seven consciousnesses is called the "Seven Buddhas.
To be able to turn back the winds of the eight kinds of crookedness and deceitful livelihoods is to transform them into the "Eight Kinds of Subtle Fragrant Winds."
To restrain the six consciousnesses so they give rise to the six pāramitās,
and to remain unstained by the six sense objects, is called the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā).
To restrain and turn back the six thieves is to transform them into the six divine kings.
Guarding the city of the Dharma;
the ten wholesome paths, the five reverences, and the seven conformities,
together with the eight kinds of subtle winds of the Buddha.
As well as the six pāramitās;
the nature of the six supernatural powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) is non-arising,
and the six spirits protect the dharmakāya.
Together these constitute forty-eight types;
when combined with the thirty-two excellent marks (*lakṣaṇa*),
they total eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*).
Chapter Eleven: Comparing Merits. The Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"If you are my foremost disciple, you are able to repay my kindness."
"You should maintain your resolve.
What is this resolve?
It is that you must be able to repay my kindness."
Each and every one of you, in accordance with my instructions and commands,
shall propagate this Dharma King,
transforming all sentient beings so that they realize the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This is for the preservation of my resolve. Why is this?
For I have heard in the past that the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara—
Furthermore, that the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One,

the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, and all the worthy sages have realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) can be known through the power of maintaining one's resolve.
One who clearly knows those with resolve possesses all the myriad practices;
one who clearly knows those without resolve [lacks them].
A single practice is not established. Why is this?
In the past, I once accompanied eighty-four thousand followers.
When comparing and weighing the merit of maintaining one's resolve,
there is nothing within these ten thousand gates of practice that surpasses this most difficult, most difficult,
and rare occurrence. Why is this?
For example, suppose there were someone who fashioned ten million pure copper images,
all in human form, which they upheld and made offerings to.
"Is this difficult?
"This is not yet difficult.
What is difficult?"
If there are good sons or good daughters who,
upon hearing the exposition of the profound and wondrous Dharma concerning the great eloquence of the heterodox and the orthodox,
immediately give rise to faith.
This is difficult. It is, for example,
like someone who fashions images of pure silver,
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, and upholds, maintains, and makes offerings to them.
Is this difficult?
This is not yet difficult.
What is difficult?
If there are good men or good women whose resolve is filial toward their teachers, monks, and parents,
exhausting their hearts and reaching the ultimate limit, [they shall attain this].
This is difficult. It is,
for example, like someone who fashions images of pure gold as numerous as the grasses and trees upon the great earth, and maintains them with devotion and makes offerings to them.
Is this difficult?
This is not yet difficult.
What is difficult?
If there are sons or daughters of good family who are able to eliminate both the self of persons and the self of phenomena,
this is indeed difficult.
Suppose, for example, there were a person who constructed a great stūpa made entirely of genuine sandalwood that reached as high as the Brahma-heaven,
and having adorned it with the seven precious jewels, they maintained and made offerings to it.
Is this difficult?
This is not yet difficult.
What is difficult?
If there are good sons or good daughters who propagate this Dharma,
transmitting it to one another in succession so that it does not become interrupted,
this would be difficult to achieve.
Suppose, for example, there were someone who constructed a magnificent house of the seven treasures that filled the entirety of Jambudvīpa and maintained it with offerings.
Would this be difficult? This, too, would not be considered difficult.
What is difficult?
If there are sons or daughters of good family who are able to rely upon the teachings and commands of their original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
"To cultivate and maintain the resolve for merit until its certain accomplishment is difficult.
At that time, there were eighty-four thousand followers within the assembly.
Upon hearing this account,
they were filled with joy and exultation,
marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence.
At that time, they together made great and far-reaching vows,
cultivating and maintaining meritorious virtues,
and practicing according to their words.
Though one may uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures, if one cannot distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox,
one will always be a person of false views and not a knower of the Dharma. If one’s mind and speech do no evil, and the body likewise commits no transgression—
by being able to maintain these three matters, one will swiftly emerge from the abyss of birth and death.
Though one may read a thousand chapters, if one does not grasp the central meaning, it is not as good as a single phrase that can lead one to the Way.
Therefore, let every student examine themselves with care;
do not waste your efforts in vain, lest you dwell forever on the path of delusion.
Xuanzang, along with my long-time teacher and Xieshe and others,
obtained within the Tathāgata’s Cave of the Seven Jewels this single fascicle of the *Tathāgata-mahāvibhāga-samyak-mithyātva-gambhīra-rahasya-kośa-sūtra*.
The Scripture on Greatly Distinguishing the Erroneous and the Correct.
